text: Good evening. My name's Jodi Cross. I'm from the firms, Aaron and Steinmetz. And I'm here today on behalf of EDTNY and Montenido and affiliates. We have also Jennifer Gallagher. She's the chief development officer of Montenido and David Resendiz. He is the VP of facilities. It's what it's known as commonly. EDTNY is seeking a license from the New York State Office of Mental Health or OMH for a community residence for eating disorder integrated treatment, also known as credit program. The program will be operated by Montenido and the proposed site is 171 Main Street in South Salem. And what we'd like to accomplish tonight is to explain who Montenido is, what they do, why 171 Main Street was selected and how Montenido can operate this type of community residence in this nature in this district. So let's start with the who. Montenido was founded in 1996. They operate 19 residential treatments in 10 different States for adults and adolescents with eating disorders. Three of those programs are in the metropolitan New York City region. Two of them are in Westchester, one on Long Island. Montenido is a for-profit tax paying entity. That means they will be paying all taxes including property taxes. Their programs are regulated by the State OMH and the program will also be regulated by OMH. All of Montenido's programs are accredited by the Joint Commission, which is the gold standard for behavioral health. And importantly, they pride themselves in operating an attractive and well-maintained property. So what does this propose residents and why is it needed? There's an estimated 3,900 adolescents with eating disorders in Westchester County alone. And there's only one credit program in the county for adolescents with just 12 beds. And that's the one operated by Montenido and Briarcliff Manor. Due to the number of adolescents in this area that are afflicted with eating disorders, they have consistently have waiting lists at the Briarcliff Manor facility. This proposed residence in South Salem would provide supervised residential care to up to 12 adolescents ages 12 to 18 with eating disorders. Eating disorders include, for example, anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating and exercise disorders. The residents stay enrolled in their home school district so there will be no additional burden on the Katona-Lewisboro schools. In order to be accepted into this program, the resident must be medically and psychiatrically stable with a primary diagnosis of an eating disorder. Typical stay, which is covered by most social insurance companies is 40 to 90 days with an average of 45 days. Services are provided by licensed therapists, other mental health professionals, nurses and registered dietitians. The majority of these programs take place indoors in the home. The most at any time there'll be 12 staff members, but we could discuss further what that staffing looks like. The staff arrives and departs from the home at staggered times in order to minimize any impacts. And there will be two staff members who stay overnight and they're awake. Even those residents who are old enough to drive, so they're 12 to 18, so not all of them are even old enough, but those that do, do not drive while they're living at this house and they won't have their cars on site. So why did Montanito choose 171 Main Street? So as I mentioned, there's a dire need for these types of programs in West Chester in the area. And Montanito looks for sites that are suitable for their program. And they combed through hundreds of listings. They looked closely at about 50 or more homes in the area and they visited approximately 35 homes looking for an appropriate location. What they look for is a large, attractive residence in a tranquil setting that provides a therapeutic environment for the residents of the home. And the home at 171 Main Street fits that bill. The house is set back 600 feet from Main Street on 4.8 acres. It's 5,200 square feet with a 1,200 square foot walkout lower level. Lots of natural light, a sufficient number of bedrooms, living areas, kitchen, dining room, et cetera. As part of this project, they will not be changing the footprint of the building and there will be renovations indoors to make the home ADA compliant. The almost five acre site has room for septic expansion and staff parking, all of which will comply with any and all applicable county and local regulations. There'll be no exterior signage, only residential lighting. Once it's there, the goal is for it to blend into the community to look like any other home. And most of the time, all the time, once these houses are established, you don't even know it's there. The whole point is for it to be a welcoming residential environment for the residents. The other thing that Montanito considers when looking at a home is what other similar residential, community residences are in the area, and this one is not near any, and I'll get to that in a little bit. So here's an aerial view of the site. As you can see, the home itself is more than 200 feet from the nearest homes, though there's a driveway here where there are homes closer to the driveway. We understand that when the leaves are down, like shown in this aerial, the driveway and the home are visible to the neighboring properties, and those are things that exist today. When Montanito acquires a property, they always prefer to add additional screening, such as evergreens, to keep areas that are most visible to the neighbors screened, and that's what they intend to do here, including along the driveway, and that will actually improve the neighbor's privacy. As you can see, when the leaves are actually on the trees, it's relatively secluded and well-screened. So the question becomes then, how do you permit a residential facility and this credit program at a site like this in four-acre zoning? New York State permits this use under the Mental Hygiene Law, the Padovan Law I mentioned earlier, and under 31.25 of the Mental Hygiene Law. The Padovan Law allows community residences in residential areas, and once they're established, they're treated for zoning purposes as single-family homes. MHL 3125 authorizes the Commissioner of OMH to promulgate regulations for programs such as the credit program. These regulations include those found in 14 NYCRR Part 594, which expressly defines the credit program as a community residence for children and adolescents with eating disorders. So again, on November 18th, we submitted a notice letter to the town under the Padovan Law, and the Padovan Law requires certain information to be set forth in that notice, and we included that information. That information is the address of the site, the type of community residence, the number of residents, community support requirements, and a list of the similar residential facilities in the area, and that list is prepared by the Department of Social Services, and we acquired it from OPWDD. And I believe at the last meeting, which I watched when this public hearing was set, the town attorney confirmed that the notice letter provided all the information that was required. So our firm's been involved with a number of these in various municipalities. Some municipalities, there's no opposition. Others, the public raises various concerns, all of which are legitimate but are unsubstantiated. You know, we understand people live in the community and they have concerns, but they're unsubstantiated concerns. We also understand that in connection with this application, there were a few letters submitted from certain neighbors of the property, and I want to address one threshold issue that was raised, which is whether a credit program is in fact covered under the Padavan law. So again, as I said before, the MHL specifically states that this is the type of residence that's permitted, and the implementing regulations also state that this is the type of residence that's permitted. And consistent with those laws and regulations, the state has applied the Padavan law to credit and eating disorder residential community residences. In fact, Montanito has received Padavan approval from New York State OMH in four different locations, two in Westchester, one in Nassau, and one in Ontario County. OMH has issued Montanito licenses to operate at three of those locations, including the credit program in Briarcliff Manor. The newest location in Ontario County is still in the process of being reviewed and it's proceeding towards licensure. Also as indication that this is in fact a community residence covered by the Padavan law, by way of example, there was an objection by the municipality on Nassau County to the location in their jurisdiction. Following that objection, the Padavan approval was recommended by an OMH administrative hearing officer. Padavan approval was then granted by the OMH commissioner, and then the approval was upheld by the Supreme Court of Nassau County. The commissioner's determination specifically acknowledged that the average length of stay was 45 to 60 days, acknowledging that Padavan applies to a program like the credit program and doesn't require some sort of permanent residency. It's also notable that the AG on behalf of OMH put in a memorandum of law in support in the litigation, asking the court to uphold the Padavan approval. So all of these actions show that this is in fact a Padavan law community residence, and we just wanted to address that fact. So the board has probably been counseled on this by your town attorney, but you have three options once a Padavan notice is submitted. And then within 40 days, the town board must either approve the proposed site, suggest suitable alternative sites, or object to the establishment of the residence at the site. MHL 4134, the Padavan law, and all the case law make it clear that there's only one basis that this site can be objected to, and that's that the establishment of the credit facility on this particular property would result in an over-concentration of the same or similar facilities so as to substantially alter the nature and character of the area. This determination would need to be based on clear and convincing evidence. It can't just be on unsubstantiated fears and opposition. It also can't be based on the fact that the jurisdiction has other community residences. And it does bear noting that no court has ever upheld an objection on the basis of over-concentration. So here, the town only has five other community residences. Here's where they're located. Here's the subject site. Here's the closest residence. It's 4.6 miles away at 8 Wacabook Road. It's a completely different area of the town. There are no other community residences in South Salem, in the South Salem Hamlet. The applicant submits then that the establishment of this home would not result in any over-concentration, much less any that would substantially alter the nature and character of the area. With regard to the second option, recommending alternative sites, those sites must be suitable for the program. At this point, we're not aware of any recommendations by the town for alternative sites, but we know that the neighbors in one of their communications raised certain alternative sites. And we do want to point out that we are only required to respond to alternative sites proposed by the town, but we always want to be good neighbors and we want to address those concerns by the neighbors. So the sites that were raised in the neighbor's first letter are not suitable alternatives for the project. They need to meet the program criteria. Among other things, they have to be adequate size. They have to have large enough rooms and they need to be located on a main road. So going through four of the sites that the neighbors suggested as alternative locations, they're not suitable for various reasons. The 33 West Lane property that was raised is too small. Rooms are too small, hallways are too small. There's a gym area in the attic, which would make it unfeasible to put an elevator in to make it ADA compliant. And there's a horse barn and paddock on the site that would be very costly to remove. The site at 1125 Route 35, although a very large property, the house itself is too small to accommodate the program. The house at 25 Beaver Road is located on a cul-de-sac. Montanito likes to locate their homes on a main road to minimize any traffic impacts. And lastly, the one Blue Stone Lane property in South Salem is new construction. It's also on a cul-de-sac and the proposed square footage is too small for the program. The other issue I want to address that was raised is that of zoning compliance. The neighbors raised that in their letter that was submitted to the board today. Admittedly, there's been no review as of yet by the building inspector because there's been nothing to review. It's not part of the Padavan process. Montanito fully understands that it must comply with all applicable zoning regulations. And we're confident that at the appropriate time when the building inspector comes to inspect the home to issue a CO, he will ensure compliance with the zoning code. And in fact, in order to be licensed by OMH, Montanito needs to demonstrate that they comply with all applicable state, county, and local laws. Otherwise they don't get their license. Again, though, that's not part of this Padavan process and the site location. Again, the only basis for an objection is an over-concentration of same or similar facilities in the area. And that establishment of this facility would cause such oversaturation as to substantially alter the nature and character of the area. Since the closest residence is almost five miles away, as you could see on the map in front of you, there's no basis here for an objection. And obviously the town here opted to hold a public hearing and Montanito always welcomes the opportunity to answer questions about the residence and is happy to do so now.
